值得閱讀的理由

  • 透過宿舍禁煮、無障礙入口等日常例子，說明表面上一視同仁的規則，可能對不同群體造成截然不同的影響。
  • 釐清「文化相對主義」與「多元文化主義」的差異，並提醒理解文化脈絡不代表所有傳統都必須被合理化。
  • 介紹團體權利、文化權與參與決策等概念，協助讀者辨別政策是在保障少數群體，還是在限制個人自由。

摘要

形式平等不一定代表人人都能參與

作者先以大學宿舍禁止在房間煮食為例：多數學生或許只是不方便煮宵夜，但若穆斯林學生在餐廳找不到清真餐點，規定便可能迫使他們在違反宿舍規則與挨餓之間抉擇。作者藉此指出，同一套規則落在不同人身上，可能有不同重量。像是入口敞開、門上寫著歡迎，門口卻有輪椅難以通行的階梯；形式上沒有拒絕任何人，不代表每個人都能真正進入。

理解文化脈絡，但不把文化視為鐵板一塊

影片以推廣公民教育為引，進一步探討多元文化。作者指出，尊重差異不能只靠個人善意或法律文字上的平等；還必須追問規則原本是為誰設計，以及它如何影響不同群體。文化相對主義提醒人們將行為放回當事人的生活脈絡理解，但脈絡只能幫助解釋，不能自動證明一切做法都正當。政治哲學家賽拉・班哈比也提醒，文化不是界線清楚、內部人人一致的固定整體，而是持續辯論、衝突與變動的過程。有人以「傳統」或「團體文化」要求所有成員服從時，往往代表的是掌握話語權者的立場，而非整個群體的共同意志。

團體權利可以是保護，也可能成為控制

理解階梯如何形成，並不會讓階梯自動消失；還需要實際改造環境，例如設置坡道。作者借用威爾・金里卡對團體權利的區分：外部保障是讓少數群體抵抗主流制度侵蝕、促進群體間平等的保護；內部限制則是團體以傳統為由，要求成員絕對服從、犧牲個人自由。以客語幼兒園為例，政府提供課程、由家長自由選擇，是保障；強迫所有客家兒童就讀且不得退出，則成了限制。台灣為本土語言編列資源、提供師資，正是從口頭允許使用語言，進一步打造實際可用的支持條件。

文化權也包括參與制定規則

即使建好了坡道，仍要追問：坡度與規格由誰決定？文化權不只是政府提供補助、課程或節慶活動，也包括少數群體參與制定直接影響自身的規則。政治理論家詹姆斯・塔利主張，多元憲政不應是人們被動接受的固定藍圖，而應是不同文化主體持續對話的過程，其核心包括相互承認、取得同意，以及維持文化延續。換言之，人們不只要問國家提供了什麼，也要問誰制定了遊戲規則。影片最後以身心障礙學生的考試規則為例：校方雖邀請專家制定延長考試時間等措施，政策上路後仍有需要頻繁如廁的學生感到被忽略，顯示規則若未納入當事人的經驗與意見，再周全也可能無法真正回應需求。字幕在此處中斷。

================================================

Take university dormitory regulations: they generally forbid cooking in rooms for fire safety reasons. It seems to treat everyone equally, as most are only limited from making instant noodles at night. But for Muslim students who require halal diets, if the cafeteria lacks a halal section, this rule forces them to choose between violating dorm policy or going hungry. The same set of rules carries completely different weights. Returning to how we examine standards, the space designed for a fictional "average adult" versus a space that is truly safe and allows everyone. to walk in with dignity have always been two different things. Commercial break: Taiwan recently had a policy to distribute cash to everyone, but what our society needs even more is a universal distribution of civic education. This is not just our reflection on social phenomena, but also our expectation for education. We are committed to rebuilding the republic, and there are two paths to doing so: one is institutional reform, and the other is the popularization of civic education . Therefore, we have launched a basic civic education series to achieve our goal of "distributing civic knowledge to everyone." This series is designed based on the Ministry of Education's current 108 Curriculum for Civics and Society,. hoping to explain complex topics simply and build a foundation for civic education together. If you have the capacity and want to support our mission , consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us a little support, or join our membership to help us go further on this path. You can also leave comments, or join our DC or TG groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Today we’re talking about multiculturalism. Everyone says we should respect diverse cultures , but what exactly does "respect" mean? And when most of us are already willing to respect the cultural systems of. minority groups, why do we still end up hurting them? There is a door wide open with a sign that says "Welcome," but when you look down, there are three steep steps at the entrance. The manager says, "We welcome everyone; the door is open, and there are no discriminatory notices posted." But if you are in a wheelchair, those three steps will keep you blocked outside. Is that really welcoming everyone? Many people say, " Oh, multiculturalism is just about. mutual respect.""As long as everyone means well and doesn't discriminate, and the law treats everyone the same, differences will naturally be treated fairly." This argument sounds fine at first, separating personal conduct as morality and public justice as law. But its major blind spot is quietly reducing complex multiculturalism to two trivial things: individual temperament and formal equality on paper.

Yet, it misses the three most critical points: who was this supposedly " impartial" law tailored to fit in the first place? Exactly. We used the example of stairs at the beginning. Why do these stairs leave certain groups of people stuck? Wheelchairs get stuck, and parents with strollers are forced to take a detour. Studying these stairs together, we realize they weren't built all at once, but rather added on piece by piece after. various events. So people say, there's a history behind why these stairs prevent some from getting up. But having a story is one thing; the fact remains that they do hinder some people from passing through. To understand a behavior, you cannot simply judge it by your own standards; you must place it back into the context of the person's life. This is cultural relativism. However, the limitation of this concept lies within that very same sentence: context can. explain something, but it does not automatically certify its legitimacy. Political philosopher Seyla Benhabib points out that many cultural debates end in a stalemate because we all share a common flaw: we are too accustomed to imagining a culture as a sphere with clear boundaries, assuming everyone in a group looks the same and thinks exactly alike. But from the outside, simplifying others this way is the easiest path, as it makes them easier to categorize and. rule. If you truly step inside that community, you will find that culture is not static, but a living process constantly debating, colliding, and full of conflict. If someone constantly plays the "this is our cultural tradition" card to silence others, it usually represents not the entire culture, but those in the community who hold the power of discourse—the elites or the elders. Take a modern workplace example: some migrant colleagues at a company propose setting aside a quiet corner in the. office as a prayer room. The HR manager smiles and replies, "Our company culture has always been secular and professional ; we don't deal with personal beliefs." This sounds neutral, but if you ask around, the engineering department doesn't mind, the sales team is all for it, and the admin staff just thinks, " Ugh, another expense report to process is such a hassle." That sacred "company culture" doesn't actually exist in any business; it’s just an excuse for managers to prioritize convenience and suppress the needs of the minority.

Packaging complex internal voices into a singular collective will is, in itself, an act of arbitrary power. We can reflect on why these obstacles were created, but simply understanding the story won't make the stairs disappear on their own. Understanding the context is just the first step, but once we see it , what methods can we actually use to let everyone in? This is what comes next . Knowing. Having understood the context. and how the stairs were built, how should we renovate so that everyone can enter? People might say, "It’s simple, just build a ramp." It bridges the height difference at the door, allowing those in wheelchairs to enter on their own. We wouldn't, and shouldn't, force everyone inside who can walk to use wheelchairs, but how do we ensure this system remains a safety net, not a tool for control, and certainly not a special privilege? When a state does more than just permit. differences, but actively invests resources and laws to protect the equal status of diverse cultural groups, it is called multiculturalism in academia. But once rights are granted to groups, problems immediately arise: what if a minority group receives state-sanctioned privileges and then turns around to oppress the vulnerable within its own ranks? Political philosopher Will Kymlicka divides group rights into two: "internal restrictions," where the group uses tradition as a pretext to demand. absolute obedience from members; and " external protections," where the group seeks space from the mainstream to resist cultural erosion by dominant laws . One is a whip directed inward; the other is a shield directed outward. Kymlicka's standard is straightforward: support external protections that promote equality between groups, but firmly oppose internal restrictions that exploit individual freedom. To give an example: if a region promotes Hakka-language kindergartens, legislation stating "the government provides Hakka classes, parents choose. freely" is an external protection; if it says "all Hakka children must enroll and cannot opt-out," it becomes a restrictive, soul-crushing internal mandate. The same budget, yet the former builds a ramp, while the latter builds a prison. In recent years, Taiwan has made local languages mandatory and offered flexible indigenous language courses for students in junior high. Merely saying " I don't mind you speaking your mother tongue" is just opening the door; allocating budgets and providing teachers so people can actually learn is what building a ramp really means.

Returning to the entrance: is a policy a protection, or is it control? First, see whether they hold a shield facing outward or a whip facing inward. But after the ramp is poured, there is a critical question we have never asked: who exactly decided the gradient and specifications of this ramp? If the ramp at the entrance is too steep, it will be hard to use; but if the slope is lowered , its length will increase, making it rarely used. So, who should decide the gradient of this ramp? Is the true. meaning of cultural rights just a list of state subsidies? Or is it about whether minority groups can voice their opinions in the decision-making process for setting rules? The people's right to preserve, use, participate in, and develop their own culture also includes participating in defining the rules that directly govern their culture. Rules of the game—this is what we call cultural rights. In the past, people easily viewed cultural rights as a list of official favors: letting you speak your native language, hosting festivals for you, or subsidizing exhibition halls— checking them off one by one, bestowed. from the top down. But political theorist James Tully completely overturned this idea. He argued that a constitution that truly embraces diversity shouldn't be a rigid, pre-defined blueprint we passively accept, but rather an ongoing deliberative process where all cultural subjects engage in continuous dialogue. He proposed three core conventions: mutual recognition (figuring out who the other is without labeling them), consent (rules affecting others must be agreed upon by them), and cultural continuity ( the original way of life remains valid. under the new system). These three principles directly flip the center of power. We used to only stare at what benefits the state gave us, but now we must look up and ask: who exactly set these rules of the game? A university wanted to set examination guidelines for students with disabilities. The administration invited various experts and scholars to a meeting and drafted a thorough procedure that included extended exam times. But the policy hit a wall on the very first day. It worked for some students, but those who needed. frequent bathroom breaks felt abandoned , because the new rules never considered the need for intermittent testing. Throughout the entire meeting, not a single student with a disability was seated at the table where the rules were being decided. This policy didn't lack professionalism or good intentions; the only thing it lacked was the substantive consent of the people involved. Back to the box on the engineering drawing that determines the gradient—who should be writing in that field? True cultural rights are about who is sitting in the seat of decision-making. The ramp is.

poured, the railings are up, and the anti-slip surface is laid perfectly; yet on the wall nearby hangs an old plaque fixed there decades ago during construction. You push the wheelchair in and out of the ramp every day, and every day you look up and see that plaque. A ramp solves the problem of whether you can get up, but a sign addresses how you are actually written into the collective memory of this society. Why is how a person is perceived a hard-nosed political issue, rather than just a matter of feelings? If a group is. fighting for more than just welfare and budgets—if they are also seeking recognition for their historical identity and dignity within the national public sphere—this is what we call the politics of recognition. Philosopher Charles Taylor put it poignantly: if society consistently imposes a distorted image upon you, it constitutes substantive oppression, effectively using institutions to imprison a person’s soul. Recognition is not a courtesy bestowed by the majority, but a fundamental human necessity. Yet, scholar Nancy Fraser pours cold water on. this; recognition alone isn't enough— the key is whether it is accompanied by actual resources. Apologies cost nothing , and replacing a sign only costs the price of the plaque. If recognition isn't tied to the redistribution of budgets, land, and power, it’s just the cheapest kind of political theater. Take , for example, a local news report on a newly completed indigenous library; while the hardware and software resources were generous, the reporter used a discriminatory term from decades ago in the front-page headline, calling it a "new home for the mountain compatriots." Resources were provided,. but the label remained unchanged, leaving that thorn still lodged in everyone's heart. In recent years, the Republic of China has taken a crucial step institutionally: in 2016, the President officially apologized to Indigenous peoples on behalf of the government, established the Indigenous Historical Justice and Transitional Justice Commission, and Article 12 of the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law further guaranteed the right to media representation, launching the Indigenous Peoples Television. What this addresses isn't just whether there are programs on TV, but who holds the microphone to describe their own identity. Returning to that old nameplate on the wall,. history does not turn its own pages; someone must personally wipe away the old words and replace them with the true name. The thresholds have been lowered, the ramps have been poured, the blueprints have been reviewed, and the old signs have been replaced; but having come this far, there remains a fundamental root problem we have yet to touch: why were those three steps built so high in the first place? As for why those three steps were built to that height, the answer isn't on the construction site, but in the inspection standards tucked away in office shelves.

. Open those regulations, and you’ll find that every step height and door width is designed for a hypothetical, average adult. This person has no disabilities, pushes no wheelchair, uses both feet to climb stairs, and the entire building is constructed to fit their physique. The regulations do allow for side doors in special cases, but those doors are so narrow and steep that a cart could tip over at any moment. Why is it that regulations claiming equality before the law and universal application always end up hitting a specific group of people the hardest? When national. uniform laws collide with the cultural customs of minority groups, how can the law preserve a path for diversity? This is called the multicultural defense. Those who oppose making room for such exceptions have a firm argument: everyone is equal before the law, and the same standard is the only true fairness. But political philosopher Iris Marion Young pointed out that this self-proclaimed neutrality is often a cover for dominant groups to package their own habits as universal standards ; that supposedly objective position, claiming to stand above everyone else,. is in itself a special privilege. From the legislator's perspective, for a law to be applied universally, they must first presuppose a typical human being in their mind. When that person is an urbanite who buys groceries at the supermarket, then labeling all hunting with firearms as a crime certainly seems impeccably just. Bias is never in the wording itself, but in the image that appears in the bureaucrat's mind when drafting the law: what does that person actually look like? Take university dormitory rules that ban cooking,. ostensibly for fire safety. It seems equal, but for most, it just means no late-night instant noodles. For Muslim students who must follow a halal diet, if the cafeteria lacks a halal section, this rule forces them to choose between violating regulations—risking expulsion —and going hungry. The same rules carry completely different weights. Returning to the examination of norms, the space provided for that fictional "average adult" and the space that is truly safe. —where everyone can walk in with their heads held high—are two different things . Next, let’s tell a real story. In that sweltering summer of July 2013, Tama Talum's 90-year-old mother was bedridden and ill. With a poor appetite, she casually said, "I really want to eat the mountain game I had as a child." As a devoted son, Tama Talum took a homemade long gun he had found in the mountains, ventured into the forest, and returned with a Formosan serow and a Reeve's muntjac. In the context of an.

individual's life and death, this was incredibly pure: a filial son, an ailing mother, and a hot, home-cooked meal. Yet , when brought into a national court, the judge viewed it through the lens of mainstream society, seeing only a series of crimes: the gun was found, not self-made, failing the legal definition of a homemade hunting rifle; the game hunted were protected species; and it was for his mother to eat, not for a tribal ritual, falling outside the exemptions of the Wildlife Conservation Act at the time. In 2014, the Taitung. District Court handed down a combined sentence of three years and six months. At that moment, a man’s simple life was abruptly severed, and the cruel gears of the state apparatus began to turn. But this case did not just vanish into the archives. The Supreme Prosecutors Office stepped on the brakes; the Prosecutor General realized that the government’s strict stance on hunting rifles effectively forced Indigenous people to use only outdated and dangerous tools, raising concerns of discrimination, and. thus filed an extraordinary appeal, which the Supreme Court later ruled to stay. In May 2021, the Constitutional Court issued Interpretation No. 803, finally pushing open the door to traditional culture by recognizing that hunting for daily subsistence is also a tradition, and declaring regulations on hunting rifles unconstitutional. That same month, the President granted a pardon, exempting him from the execution of his sentence. Then, in 2023, the government announced new regulations on hunting rifles, sparking an outcry across tribal communities nationwide,. which led officials to hold ten forums across the country. Finally, in March 2024, the Supreme Court officially acquitted Wang Guang.   • 透過宿舍禁煮、無障礙入口等日常例子，說明表面上一視同仁的規則，可能對不同群體造成截然不同的影響。

摘要

形式平等不一定代表人人都能參與

作者先以大學宿舍禁止在房間煮食為例：多數學生或許只是不方便煮宵夜，但若穆斯林學生在餐廳找不到清真餐點，規定便可能迫使他們在違反宿舍規則與挨餓之間抉擇。作者藉此指出，同一套規則落在不同人身上，可能有不同重量。像是入口敞開、門上寫著歡迎，門口卻有輪椅難以通行的階梯；形式上沒有拒絕任何人，不代表每個人都能真正進入。

理解文化脈絡，但不把文化視為鐵板一塊

影片以推廣公民教育為引，進一步探討多元文化。作者指出，尊重差異不能只靠個人善意或法律文字上的平等；還必須追問規則原本是為誰設計，以及它如何影響不同群體。文化相對主義提醒人們將行為放回當事人的生活脈絡理解，但脈絡只能幫助解釋，不能自動證明一切做法都正當。政治哲學家賽拉・班哈比也提醒，文化不是界線清楚、內部人人一致的固定整體，而是持續辯論、衝突與變動的過程。有人以「傳統」或「團體文化」要求所有成員服從時，往往代表的是掌握話語權者的立場，而非整個群體的共同意志。

理解階梯如何形成，並不會讓階梯自動消失；還需要實際改造環境，例如設置坡道。作者借用威爾・金里卡對團體權利的區分：外部保障是讓少數群體抵抗主流制度侵蝕、促進群體間平等的保護；內部限制則是團體以傳統為由，要求成員絕對服從、犧牲個人自由。以客語幼兒園為例，政府提供課程、由家長自由選擇，是保障；強迫所有客家兒童就讀且不得退出，則成了限制。台灣為本土語言編列資源、提供師資，正是從口頭允許使用語言，進一步打造實際可用的支持條件。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 透過宿舍禁煮、無障礙入口等日常例子，說明表面上一視同仁的規則，可能對不同群體造成截然不同的影響。
  • 釐清「文化相對主義」與「多元文化主義」的差異，並提醒理解文化脈絡不代表所有傳統都必須被合理化。
  • 介紹團體權利、文化權與參與決策等概念，協助讀者辨別政策是在保障少數群體，還是在限制個人自由。

摘要

形式平等不一定代表人人都能參與

作者先以大學宿舍禁止在房間煮食為例：多數學生或許只是不方便煮宵夜，但若穆斯林學生在餐廳找不到清真餐點，規定便可能迫使他們在違反宿舍規則與挨餓之間抉擇。作者藉此指出，同一套規則落在不同人身上，可能有不同重量。像是入口敞開、門上寫著歡迎，門口卻有輪椅難以通行的階梯；形式上沒有拒絕任何人，不代表每個人都能真正進入。

理解文化脈絡，但不把文化視為鐵板一塊

影片以推廣公民教育為引，進一步探討多元文化。作者指出，尊重差異不能只靠個人善意或法律文字上的平等；還必須追問規則原本是為誰設計，以及它如何影響不同群體。文化相對主義提醒人們將行為放回當事人的生活脈絡理解，但脈絡只能幫助解釋，不能自動證明一切做法都正當。政治哲學家賽拉・班哈比也提醒，文化不是界線清楚、內部人人一致的固定整體，而是持續辯論、衝突與變動的過程。有人以「傳統」或「團體文化」要求所有成員服從時，往往代表的是掌握話語權者的立場，而非整個群體的共同意志。

團體權利可以是保護，也可能成為控制

理解階梯如何形成，並不會讓階梯自動消失；還需要實際改造環境，例如設置坡道。作者借用威爾・金里卡對團體權利的區分：外部保障是讓少數群體抵抗主流制度侵蝕、促進群體間平等的保護；內部限制則是團體以傳統為由，要求成員絕對服從、犧牲個人自由。以客語幼兒園為例，政府提供課程、由家長自由選擇，是保障；強迫所有客家兒童就讀且不得退出，則成了限制。台灣為本土語言編列資源、提供師資，正是從口頭允許使用語言，進一步打造實際可用的支持條件。

文化權也包括參與制定規則

即使建好了坡道，仍要追問：坡度與規格由誰決定？文化權不只是政府提供補助、課程或節慶活動，也包括少數群體參與制定直接影響自身的規則。政治理論家詹姆斯・塔利主張，多元憲政不應是人們被動接受的固定藍圖，而應是不同文化主體持續對話的過程，其核心包括相互承認、取得同意，以及維持文化延續。換言之，人們不只要問國家提供了什麼，也要問誰制定了遊戲規則。影片最後以身心障礙學生的考試規則為例：校方雖邀請專家制定延長考試時間等措施，政策上路後仍有需要頻繁如廁的學生感到被忽略，顯示規則若未納入當事人的經驗與意見，再周全也可能無法真正回應需求。字幕在此處中斷。

================================================

Take university dormitory regulations: they generally forbid cooking in rooms for fire safety reasons. It seems to treat everyone equally, as most are only limited from making instant noodles at night. But for Muslim students who require halal diets, if the cafeteria lacks a halal section, this rule forces them to choose between violating dorm policy or going hungry. The same set of rules carries completely different weights. Returning to how we examine standards, the space designed for a fictional "average adult" versus a space that is truly safe and allows everyone. to walk in with dignity have always been two different things. Commercial break: Taiwan recently had a policy to distribute cash to everyone, but what our society needs even more is a universal distribution of civic education. This is not just our reflection on social phenomena, but also our expectation for education. We are committed to rebuilding the republic, and there are two paths to doing so: one is institutional reform, and the other is the popularization of civic education . Therefore, we have launched a basic civic education series to achieve our goal of "distributing civic knowledge to everyone." This series is designed based on the Ministry of Education's current 108 Curriculum for Civics and Society,. hoping to explain complex topics simply and build a foundation for civic education together. If you have the capacity and want to support our mission , consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us a little support, or join our membership to help us go further on this path. You can also leave comments, or join our DC or TG groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Today we’re talking about multiculturalism. Everyone says we should respect diverse cultures , but what exactly does "respect" mean? And when most of us are already willing to respect the cultural systems of. minority groups, why do we still end up hurting them? There is a door wide open with a sign that says "Welcome," but when you look down, there are three steep steps at the entrance. The manager says, "We welcome everyone; the door is open, and there are no discriminatory notices posted." But if you are in a wheelchair, those three steps will keep you blocked outside. Is that really welcoming everyone? Many people say, " Oh, multiculturalism is just about. mutual respect.""As long as everyone means well and doesn't discriminate, and the law treats everyone the same, differences will naturally be treated fairly." This argument sounds fine at first, separating personal conduct as morality and public justice as law. But its major blind spot is quietly reducing complex multiculturalism to two trivial things: individual temperament and formal equality on paper.

Yet, it misses the three most critical points: who was this supposedly " impartial" law tailored to fit in the first place? Exactly. We used the example of stairs at the beginning. Why do these stairs leave certain groups of people stuck? Wheelchairs get stuck, and parents with strollers are forced to take a detour. Studying these stairs together, we realize they weren't built all at once, but rather added on piece by piece after. various events. So people say, there's a history behind why these stairs prevent some from getting up. But having a story is one thing; the fact remains that they do hinder some people from passing through. To understand a behavior, you cannot simply judge it by your own standards; you must place it back into the context of the person's life. This is cultural relativism. However, the limitation of this concept lies within that very same sentence: context can. explain something, but it does not automatically certify its legitimacy. Political philosopher Seyla Benhabib points out that many cultural debates end in a stalemate because we all share a common flaw: we are too accustomed to imagining a culture as a sphere with clear boundaries, assuming everyone in a group looks the same and thinks exactly alike. But from the outside, simplifying others this way is the easiest path, as it makes them easier to categorize and. rule. If you truly step inside that community, you will find that culture is not static, but a living process constantly debating, colliding, and full of conflict. If someone constantly plays the "this is our cultural tradition" card to silence others, it usually represents not the entire culture, but those in the community who hold the power of discourse—the elites or the elders. Take a modern workplace example: some migrant colleagues at a company propose setting aside a quiet corner in the. office as a prayer room. The HR manager smiles and replies, "Our company culture has always been secular and professional ; we don't deal with personal beliefs." This sounds neutral, but if you ask around, the engineering department doesn't mind, the sales team is all for it, and the admin staff just thinks, " Ugh, another expense report to process is such a hassle." That sacred "company culture" doesn't actually exist in any business; it’s just an excuse for managers to prioritize convenience and suppress the needs of the minority.

Packaging complex internal voices into a singular collective will is, in itself, an act of arbitrary power. We can reflect on why these obstacles were created, but simply understanding the story won't make the stairs disappear on their own. Understanding the context is just the first step, but once we see it , what methods can we actually use to let everyone in? This is what comes next . Knowing. Having understood the context. and how the stairs were built, how should we renovate so that everyone can enter? People might say, "It’s simple, just build a ramp." It bridges the height difference at the door, allowing those in wheelchairs to enter on their own. We wouldn't, and shouldn't, force everyone inside who can walk to use wheelchairs, but how do we ensure this system remains a safety net, not a tool for control, and certainly not a special privilege? When a state does more than just permit. differences, but actively invests resources and laws to protect the equal status of diverse cultural groups, it is called multiculturalism in academia. But once rights are granted to groups, problems immediately arise: what if a minority group receives state-sanctioned privileges and then turns around to oppress the vulnerable within its own ranks? Political philosopher Will Kymlicka divides group rights into two: "internal restrictions," where the group uses tradition as a pretext to demand. absolute obedience from members; and " external protections," where the group seeks space from the mainstream to resist cultural erosion by dominant laws . One is a whip directed inward; the other is a shield directed outward. Kymlicka's standard is straightforward: support external protections that promote equality between groups, but firmly oppose internal restrictions that exploit individual freedom. To give an example: if a region promotes Hakka-language kindergartens, legislation stating "the government provides Hakka classes, parents choose. freely" is an external protection; if it says "all Hakka children must enroll and cannot opt-out," it becomes a restrictive, soul-crushing internal mandate. The same budget, yet the former builds a ramp, while the latter builds a prison. In recent years, Taiwan has made local languages mandatory and offered flexible indigenous language courses for students in junior high. Merely saying " I don't mind you speaking your mother tongue" is just opening the door; allocating budgets and providing teachers so people can actually learn is what building a ramp really means.

Returning to the entrance: is a policy a protection, or is it control? First, see whether they hold a shield facing outward or a whip facing inward. But after the ramp is poured, there is a critical question we have never asked: who exactly decided the gradient and specifications of this ramp? If the ramp at the entrance is too steep, it will be hard to use; but if the slope is lowered , its length will increase, making it rarely used. So, who should decide the gradient of this ramp? Is the true. meaning of cultural rights just a list of state subsidies? Or is it about whether minority groups can voice their opinions in the decision-making process for setting rules? The people's right to preserve, use, participate in, and develop their own culture also includes participating in defining the rules that directly govern their culture. Rules of the game—this is what we call cultural rights. In the past, people easily viewed cultural rights as a list of official favors: letting you speak your native language, hosting festivals for you, or subsidizing exhibition halls— checking them off one by one, bestowed. from the top down. But political theorist James Tully completely overturned this idea. He argued that a constitution that truly embraces diversity shouldn't be a rigid, pre-defined blueprint we passively accept, but rather an ongoing deliberative process where all cultural subjects engage in continuous dialogue. He proposed three core conventions: mutual recognition (figuring out who the other is without labeling them), consent (rules affecting others must be agreed upon by them), and cultural continuity ( the original way of life remains valid. under the new system). These three principles directly flip the center of power. We used to only stare at what benefits the state gave us, but now we must look up and ask: who exactly set these rules of the game? A university wanted to set examination guidelines for students with disabilities. The administration invited various experts and scholars to a meeting and drafted a thorough procedure that included extended exam times. But the policy hit a wall on the very first day. It worked for some students, but those who needed. frequent bathroom breaks felt abandoned , because the new rules never considered the need for intermittent testing. Throughout the entire meeting, not a single student with a disability was seated at the table where the rules were being decided. This policy didn't lack professionalism or good intentions; the only thing it lacked was the substantive consent of the people involved. Back to the box on the engineering drawing that determines the gradient—who should be writing in that field? True cultural rights are about who is sitting in the seat of decision-making. The ramp is.

poured, the railings are up, and the anti-slip surface is laid perfectly; yet on the wall nearby hangs an old plaque fixed there decades ago during construction. You push the wheelchair in and out of the ramp every day, and every day you look up and see that plaque. A ramp solves the problem of whether you can get up, but a sign addresses how you are actually written into the collective memory of this society. Why is how a person is perceived a hard-nosed political issue, rather than just a matter of feelings? If a group is. fighting for more than just welfare and budgets—if they are also seeking recognition for their historical identity and dignity within the national public sphere—this is what we call the politics of recognition. Philosopher Charles Taylor put it poignantly: if society consistently imposes a distorted image upon you, it constitutes substantive oppression, effectively using institutions to imprison a person’s soul. Recognition is not a courtesy bestowed by the majority, but a fundamental human necessity. Yet, scholar Nancy Fraser pours cold water on. this; recognition alone isn't enough— the key is whether it is accompanied by actual resources. Apologies cost nothing , and replacing a sign only costs the price of the plaque. If recognition isn't tied to the redistribution of budgets, land, and power, it’s just the cheapest kind of political theater. Take , for example, a local news report on a newly completed indigenous library; while the hardware and software resources were generous, the reporter used a discriminatory term from decades ago in the front-page headline, calling it a "new home for the mountain compatriots." Resources were provided,. but the label remained unchanged, leaving that thorn still lodged in everyone's heart. In recent years, the Republic of China has taken a crucial step institutionally: in 2016, the President officially apologized to Indigenous peoples on behalf of the government, established the Indigenous Historical Justice and Transitional Justice Commission, and Article 12 of the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law further guaranteed the right to media representation, launching the Indigenous Peoples Television. What this addresses isn't just whether there are programs on TV, but who holds the microphone to describe their own identity. Returning to that old nameplate on the wall,. history does not turn its own pages; someone must personally wipe away the old words and replace them with the true name. The thresholds have been lowered, the ramps have been poured, the blueprints have been reviewed, and the old signs have been replaced; but having come this far, there remains a fundamental root problem we have yet to touch: why were those three steps built so high in the first place? As for why those three steps were built to that height, the answer isn't on the construction site, but in the inspection standards tucked away in office shelves.

. Open those regulations, and you’ll find that every step height and door width is designed for a hypothetical, average adult. This person has no disabilities, pushes no wheelchair, uses both feet to climb stairs, and the entire building is constructed to fit their physique. The regulations do allow for side doors in special cases, but those doors are so narrow and steep that a cart could tip over at any moment. Why is it that regulations claiming equality before the law and universal application always end up hitting a specific group of people the hardest? When national. uniform laws collide with the cultural customs of minority groups, how can the law preserve a path for diversity? This is called the multicultural defense. Those who oppose making room for such exceptions have a firm argument: everyone is equal before the law, and the same standard is the only true fairness. But political philosopher Iris Marion Young pointed out that this self-proclaimed neutrality is often a cover for dominant groups to package their own habits as universal standards ; that supposedly objective position, claiming to stand above everyone else,. is in itself a special privilege. From the legislator's perspective, for a law to be applied universally, they must first presuppose a typical human being in their mind. When that person is an urbanite who buys groceries at the supermarket, then labeling all hunting with firearms as a crime certainly seems impeccably just. Bias is never in the wording itself, but in the image that appears in the bureaucrat's mind when drafting the law: what does that person actually look like? Take university dormitory rules that ban cooking,. ostensibly for fire safety. It seems equal, but for most, it just means no late-night instant noodles. For Muslim students who must follow a halal diet, if the cafeteria lacks a halal section, this rule forces them to choose between violating regulations—risking expulsion —and going hungry. The same rules carry completely different weights. Returning to the examination of norms, the space provided for that fictional "average adult" and the space that is truly safe. —where everyone can walk in with their heads held high—are two different things . Next, let’s tell a real story. In that sweltering summer of July 2013, Tama Talum's 90-year-old mother was bedridden and ill. With a poor appetite, she casually said, "I really want to eat the mountain game I had as a child." As a devoted son, Tama Talum took a homemade long gun he had found in the mountains, ventured into the forest, and returned with a Formosan serow and a Reeve's muntjac. In the context of an.

individual's life and death, this was incredibly pure: a filial son, an ailing mother, and a hot, home-cooked meal. Yet , when brought into a national court, the judge viewed it through the lens of mainstream society, seeing only a series of crimes: the gun was found, not self-made, failing the legal definition of a homemade hunting rifle; the game hunted were protected species; and it was for his mother to eat, not for a tribal ritual, falling outside the exemptions of the Wildlife Conservation Act at the time. In 2014, the Taitung. District Court handed down a combined sentence of three years and six months. At that moment, a man’s simple life was abruptly severed, and the cruel gears of the state apparatus began to turn. But this case did not just vanish into the archives. The Supreme Prosecutors Office stepped on the brakes; the Prosecutor General realized that the government’s strict stance on hunting rifles effectively forced Indigenous people to use only outdated and dangerous tools, raising concerns of discrimination, and. thus filed an extraordinary appeal, which the Supreme Court later ruled to stay. In May 2021, the Constitutional Court issued Interpretation No. 803, finally pushing open the door to traditional culture by recognizing that hunting for daily subsistence is also a tradition, and declaring regulations on hunting rifles unconstitutional. That same month, the President granted a pardon, exempting him from the execution of his sentence. Then, in 2023, the government announced new regulations on hunting rifles, sparking an outcry across tribal communities nationwide,. which led officials to hold ten forums across the country. Finally, in March 2024, the Supreme Court officially acquitted Wang Guang. In early 2025, the Legislative Yuan further amended the law to decriminalize unauthorized hunting, changing it to an administrative penalty , and the competent authority subsequently issued new hunting rifle regulations that incorporate a dual-track inspection system. From the time Wang Guang carried his rifle up the mountain in 2013 to the court’s acquittal in 2024, the eleven years and eight months of time did not just secure. one man’s innocence; the threshold at his doorway was leveled, and the concrete ramp was finally completed. But the reason this ramp is usable today is not because the majority was in a good mood and decided to show a little kindness, but because at a certain final decision-making meeting, those who actually walk this path were finally invited into the drawing room. To have a seat. Inviting users into design and legislative meetings never guarantees a perfect blueprint. The only.

thing it guarantees is that the blind spots those sitting in air-conditioned rooms could never imagine will be caught earlier and more effectively, and those who catch the problems have the power to raise their hands before the blueprint is finalized. Institutional protection is not an act of charity; at its core, it is an arrangement that allows those affected by regulations to legally voice their objections. A-Niu has one final question for everyone to ponder: Article 8 of the Republic of China’s Basic Law on Indigenous Culture explicitly states that when formulating cultural and. language policies for different ethnic groups, representatives of those groups must be meaningfully involved. Supporters believe this marks the point where cultural rights finally transition from slogans into legal procedure, but opponents raise questions: in a community already filled with internal generational disputes and class divisions, who is actually qualified to call themselves a representative? Can the highly respected elders chosen by the 330 tribal councils truly represent young indigenous people living in urban areas who can barely speak their mother tongue? If you were the architect of the. system, how would you design a mechanism that ensures diverse voices are heard without letting public policy become paralyzed by internal representation issues? We welcome you to share your thoughts. Our channel has always been committed to the idea of remaking the republic, hoping to awaken a focus on democratic values through civic awareness and historical education.
